item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] What freedom feels like after Gaza
item.description:
What freedom feels like after Gaza

Submitted by Lubna Masarwa on Thu, 08/06/2026 - 18:40
In London, I meet two Palestinian friends who survived the genocide. Hanging over us is the same bewilderment at a world that appears normal yet has also normalised the hell we left
Palestinians wait to leave Gaza for Egypt via the Rafah crossing, in Khan Younis on 19 March 2026 (Bashar Taleb/AFP)
Off

"I wasn't allowed to take anything with me when I left Gaza," Omar tells me.

"You were only allowed to go out with your T-shirt and trousers. Otherwise, I wanted to bring you a gift: a home blessing made of wood from Gaza - something we put at the entrance to bless our homes.

"You know, home means a lot to me, especially after our house, where I was born and grew up, was bombed.

"So, instead, I brought you a traditional Irish home blessing from Dublin. It has a meaning, too," he says, as he hands it to me.

I meet with Omar and Saleem at King's Cross in London. Both survived the genocide and managed to leave Gaza; one went to Dublin and one to London.

Freedom is beautiful, I say, as we walk.

But the same cloud hangs over the three of us. It is bewilderment at a world that appears normal, yet has also normalised the hellhole all three of us have left behind.

When Omar arrived at Dublin airport, he kept looking around himself, wondering if anyone was going to beat or arrest him.

He doesn't like airports.

Hiding our passports

"When I'm in line at the airport, I hide my passport. It's a refugee passport and has a different colour from others.

"The moment they see it, their faces change. And they treat you differently. As if they are paying for the air you breathe."

I know the feeling. When I fly through Ben Gurion Airport, everything goes fine until they look at my passport and find out I am a class B citizen.

'When I'm in line at the airport, I hide my passport. It's a refugee passport... The moment they see it, their faces change. And they treat you differently.'

Saleem hides his passport until the last moment.

When he flew from Berlin to London, the German border guard kept asking for more documents.

"He shouted at me loudly and, in front of everyone, said: 'You are not a British citizen'," Saleem recalls.

"I never wanted to be a British citizen. I loved my life in Gaza. I miss my parents, the Friday gatherings, and my friends. I miss speaking my language, going to the beach, and hanging out with my friends.

"I didn't take any money from the UK. I am working and paying taxes. All I want is for Britain to stop funding the genocide so I can go home."

News from Palestine

Omar and Saleem ask me about news from Palestine.

A week before I visited London, I was stuck on the road from Ramallah to Jerusalem for four hours. It is a drive that usually takes 20 minutes in normal cities.

It was the second day of the Muslim holiday of Eid, and many families were on their way to visit relatives.

Still, the army decided to close the gate without prior notice, and hundreds of cars were stuck all evening, with no way to move forward or backwards.

Tell killings: Does the right of self-defence apply only to Jews?
Read More »

Mothers decided to leave their cars and set off on foot, weaving through cars and leading their children, who were dressed in their Eid clothing, to nearby villages.

Desperate drivers of different ages, some of them maybe on their way to the hospital, were stuck for hours, while no one told them how long it would take.

There are now nearly 1,000 documented barriers in cities and towns in the West Bank, gates at the exits of villages and towns, creating ghettos that make daily life impossible for more than three million Palestinians.

The army closes and opens the gates on a whim. Palestinians have to manage life around it and find alternative ways.

I look around me in London. I half expect to see Israeli flags, armed groups in the streets, slogans about winning the war: "With God's help, we will win."

This morning, among the thousand news updates and messages I received, I come across a photo of three children aged between two and five. They were soaked in their own blood after being killed during the night while they slept in their tent.

No one has spoken about Gaza since the ceasefire. At the same time, Israel keeps bombing and killing civilians day and night.

Another family, another piece of news, gets lost in the summertime, with people rushing to plan their summer holidays.

Night raids

In the West Bank, I speak with a young mother of five in the village of Tell.

This village made the news after a settler raid that ended with the killing of four Palestinians, as well as an Israeli army officer and a settlement security guard.

Since the incident, Naheel's family and her five children have not left the house. Not even for the yard, she says.

They all sit in one room, awake all night, and go to sleep in the morning.

Follow Middle East Eye's live coverage of Israel's genocide in Gaza

"Nights are a time of settler and army raids, and we must stay awake," she tells me.

They update each other by WhatsApp on where the night raids are happening. They all know there is no one to protect them.

"What do you tell your five-year-old son?" I ask her.

"I tell my five-year-old son the truth. I do not hide reality from him. If there is something he cannot fully understand, I explain it more simply. I tell him that the settlers have come into the area and might attack people.

"When he asks why they beat or attacked people, I try to explain it through a simple story that he can understand. I do not want him to be disconnected from reality, because he could find himself in the middle of such an event, and that would affect him even more psychologically. If he understands, even to some extent, what is happening, I believe it is easier on him emotionally.

"My children have already experienced an army raid and the arrest of their father. When he was released two years later, the children looked at him and said: 'Dad, you don't look like yourself'."

Omar, Saleem and I look at the families sitting with their children, watching a film on a public screen by the canal. Other children are playing in the water fountains.

The three of us stand and look at the scene, almost in incomprehension.

Omar then tells me: "When I first moved to Dublin, I found one sock in my clothes that belonged to my mother; it may have got into my suitcase by mistake.

"But then for the whole year I couldn't sleep without it. I put it under my pillow.

"Sometimes I was like a little boy, holding this sock and weeping," he says. "I miss my mother and my life in Gaza."

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] US Senator Fetterman struggles to defend support for Israel as progressives win big
item.description:
US Senator Fetterman struggles to defend support for Israel as progressives win big

Submitted by MEE staff on Thu, 08/06/2026 - 17:17
In what was at times a bizarre exchange with TV host Jon Stewart, Fetterman pivoted to exaggerated or unrelated talking points
Pennsylvania Democratic Senator John Fetterman, right, speaks to television host and podcaster Jon Stewart on The Weekly Show with Jon Stewart, on 4 August 2026 (Screengrab)
Off

The staunchly pro-Israel Democratic Senator John Fetterman has told television host and podcaster Jon Stewart that he would rather lose support in his own party than turn his back on Israel for any reason. 

The comments are striking because they come at a time when progressive Democrats who are vocal on Palestinian rights are making substantial election gains around the country.

On Wednesday, in the key battleground state of Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed beat out a pro-Israel candidate funded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, moving one step closer to becoming the first Muslim senator in US history.

Even Rahm Emanuel, a former advisor to Barack Obama whose father was part of the Irgun militia that ransacked Palestinian homes and killed their residents in 1948, has acknowledged the Democratic Party needs to move away from unconditional support for Israel. 

"There are a lot of stories of how I've become increasingly more unpopular with Democrats in my state. And I'm aware of it. But these were all very specific choices," Fetterman told Stewart in an interview recorded on Tuesday.

"I would rather have people know what I happen to believe... My proud standing with Israel through everything after 10/7 has put me at odds more than anything," he added, referencing the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, which prompted the nearly three-year-long assault by Israel on Gaza that holocaust experts and the United Nations have labelled a genocide. 

While many older, centrist Democrats can feel the same, Fetterman has always been an outlier in the party. He has represented the battleground state of Pennsylvania in the Senate since January 2023 and largely votes alongside Democrats, except when it comes to issues related to Israel.

Democratic hopeful Rahm Emanuel calls for end to unconditional US aid to Israel
Read More »

The 56-year-old has voiced his disdain for the widespread college campus protests in 2024 that called for an end to Israel's genocide in Gaza, supported President Donald Trump's war on Iran, and has been entirely immovable on unconditional foreign aid to Israel, which he calls a "special ally".

"So for you, you could agree with [Democrats] 90 percent, but Israel is the red line," Stewart told Fetterman.

"Absolutely. Israel, for me, like I can't ever turn my back to Israel after where it's at," Fetterman said.

"I mean no disrespect on this, but that is not our country," Stewart pushed back.

Fetterman responded by referencing growing antisemitism in America.

"The Jewish community and Israel are not the same thing, brother man. They're not - that is not the same thing," replied Stewart, who is Jewish, while Fetterman is not. 

"If I have to pick a side for after 10/7 and after Iran, I'm always going to stand with Israel," the senator said. "I'm always going to vote and support whatever that's necessary to protect themselves and to prosecute Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran too."

"If anyone in the Democrat Party is fine with Iran building a nuclear bomb, I disagree with that person," he added.

"I think you're caricaturing the issue," Stewart said. "Is there anything you would criticise Israel about?"

"No."

Talking points

Stewart tried to elicit empathy from Fetterman on the more than 22,000 children that have been killed by Israel in Gaza.

"It's awful," the senator acknowledged.

"Would you say everything Israel is doing is for their own self-defence?" Stewart asked.

"Destroying its enemies, yeah," Fetterman replied

"Flattening a tiny area and pushing two million people into 30 to 35 to 40 percent of that territory, and having a siege of that area. Is that in their self-defence?"

After Michigan upset, Aipac looks to back Republican candidate against Abdul El-Sayed
Read More »

"People forget that Hamas were just rapists and they were terrorising and killing civilians," Fetterman said.

To date, there has been no first-person or direct eyewitness evidence documented by international organisations that rape was committed during the dawn attack on 7 October 2023. 

When asked if what is happening in Gaza is a genocide, Fetterman said that "by definition", only the Jewish community has "experienced a true, true genocide".

"If Israel's goal was to eliminate as many Palestinians as possible, they could have accomplished that a long time ago," the senator declared.

"Just because you're killing a group slowly doesn't mean you're not killing a group," Stewart countered.

Fetterman explained that the term "Zionist" is now being used as a "slur" among some people in the Democratic Party, and that he himself has been hounded by protesters calling him a "Zio". 

He then asked why university students were not protesting against the Iranian government for its killing of protesters during a mass uprising earlier this year.

"That's because we don't consider Iran an ally. We don't give money to Iran. We don't give billions of dollars a year to Iran. We sanction them," Stewart said.

Fetterman pivoted to how much Israel has actually been helping Gaza.

"Actually, Hamas has been stealing all of the aid," he said.

The former head of the World Food Programme, an American citizen and a Republican, acknowledged last year that there was no evidence that Hamas members were attacking or stealing from the limited aid trucks entering the enclave.

Confusion

The interview took a bizarre turn at times, when Fetterman seemed to be trying to recall, unsuccessfully, talking points or even structure his answer. He would veer into another topic entirely, almost like he didn't understand the question, rather than trying to evade it. 

In his final year as lieutenant governor in Pennsylvania - some three months before he beat television personality Mehmet Oz to win the Senate seat in November 2022 - Fetterman suffered a stroke. As he recovered and made public appearances, he seemed incapable of articulating himself in interviews, or indeed in the candidates' debate he had with Oz.

Fetterman still ended up winning with 51 percent of the vote.

He was sworn into office at the US Capitol in January 2023, and a month later, revealed he had been suffering from depression, leading him to be hospitalised for two months. The announcement was lauded by his colleagues as a brave admission on how men in particular should handle their mental health. 

During the 75-minute interview with Stewart, about half the time was spent discussing the unpopular state of the Democratic Party establishment, the rising Democratic Socialists who have galvanised voters, and the economic status quo that has turned Americans away from centrist politicians.

From Michigan to Missouri: Democratic primaries deliver mixed bag on Israel and Gaza
Read More »

"Don't you think this new sort of energy and economic populism is a response to that?" Stewart asked.

"Well, what is that? Is that socialism... communism?" Fetterman responded, arguing that Democrats with socialist policy platforms cannot defeat Republicans in swing states, which can go either way at elections.

"That sounds like a caricature," Stewart fired back. "El-Sayed.. wants to ban corporate money. Wants higher taxes on billionaires for housing and education, Medicare for all. You know, when you say that's communism, that feels like a caricature."

"No, no, I never said that," Fetterman said.

"I call real communists that are cheering for communism, people like Hassan Piker, for example. You know, he's a big, big influence."

"I don't think it's a communist. I think he said he's socialist," Stewart said of the political influencer and Twitch streamer who has backed Sayed and joined him at rallies.

"But the point being... capitalism, as it is being practised in America, is increasing inequality and leaving too many people behind," Stewart explained.

"I return it back to this idea that AI is transforming the world, whether you like it or not," Fetterman replied, in one of the stranger moments in the discussion.

"The second we hinder our own ability to develop these kinds of tools, the Chinese will seize the lead," he continued.

When Stewart tried to get him back on track, Fetterman said that while he agrees that money should be taken out of politics in the US - as Sayed and others have campaigned - Piker remains "pro-Hamas", and so Fetterman cannot support the candidates that Piker endorses.

"I feel like you're caricaturing people's views if they're critical of Israel. If someone says, 'I think Hamas and Israel are both criminal'... how is that pro-Hamas?" Stewart asked.

"What I would say is... our party is starting to elect people that are going to struggle to win in the kinds of places that are going to define who's going to win in [20]28," Fetterman said.

"When we live in a very divided country right now, I think the responsibility is to police your own ranks."

With a pair of executive orders on Thursday, Donald Trump has tried – once again – to undermine the guarantee of birthright citizenship, a right enshrined in the US constitution and reaffirmed by the supreme court just five weeks ago.

The orders attempt to broaden the categories of children who would be ineligible for automatic US citizenship and ban so-called “birth tourism”, which the president claimed is practiced by “hundreds of thousands” of people.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harms to children’s mental health
item.description:
Ruling comes as part of second phase of landmark trial that found social media company enabled harm against users

A New Mexico court has ordered Meta, the parent company of Facebook, to pay $567m into a fund aimed at redressing adverse mental health impacts from the social media giant’s platforms.

The Thursday ruling comes as a part of the second phase of a landmark trial the social media giant lost in March. At the time, a jury found that the company knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms, and imposed the maximum penalty: a $375m fine.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Justin Pearson and Brent Taylor win primaries for key Tennessee House seat
item.description:
Nominees to face off in November in redistricted seat central to Trump’s bid to retain slim Republican majority

Tennessee primary voters picked a pair of Memphis-area lawmakers to square off in a dramatically reconfigured US House seat central to Donald Trump’s plan to try to hold on to a slim Republican majority in the midterm congressional elections.

Republicans chose state senator Brent Taylor, who was endorsed by Trump, to be their nominee in the revamped 9th congressional district. Democrats picked state representative Justin Pearson, who gained national prominence three years ago when he was expelled from the Tennessee House for protesting in support of gun control measures.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] US Senator Fetterman struggles to defend support for Israel as progressives win big
item.description:
US Senator Fetterman struggles to defend support for Israel as progressives win big

The staunchly pro-Israel Democratic Senator John Fetterman has told television host and podcaster Jon Stewart that he would rather lose support in his own party than turn his back on Israel for any reason. 

The comments are striking because they come at a time when progressive Democrats who are vocal on Palestinian rights are making substantial election gains around the country.

On Wednesday, in the key battleground state of Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed beat out a pro-Israel candidate funded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, moving one step closer to becoming the first Muslim senator in US history.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Israeli army withdraws after two-day raid in East Jerusalem refugee camp
item.description:
Israeli army withdraws after two-day raid in East Jerusalem refugee camp

The Israeli army withdrew from the Qalandiya refugee camp after a large-scale raid that left at least 51 Palestinians wounded. 

The operation began on Wednesday, when dozens of military vehicles stormed the camp before dawn, carrying boxes, equipment and maps.

Soldiers deployed across several neighbourhoods as home raids and searches continued. Meanwhile, a number of homes and other buildings were seized and turned into detention and field interrogation centres. 

According to the Palestinian Prisoners’ Society, Israeli forces had detained or subjected more than 60 Palestinians, including women and children, to field interrogation.

Qalandiya camp is home to more than 15,000 Palestinian refugees living in a densely populated area. 

Its location between Jerusalem and Ramallah, close to Israeli settlements and other Israeli-controlled areas, has made it a frequent target of Israeli military raids over the years.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Trump unbound: the making of an imperial presidency – podcast
item.description:
Donald Trump’s second term is unlike his first. The politicians who challenged him are gone. The lawyers who once pushed back now choose their battles.
